query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In initially single-phase, compositionally complex FCC high-entropy alloys, brittle behavior emerges not from grain-boundary precipitation but from intragranular chemical short-range order (SRO) that increases slip planarity and reduces crack-tip strain hardening. When SRO exceeds a percolation-like correlation length, local stacking-fault-energy (SFE) fluctuations and athermal friction-stress heterogeneity promote long, persistent slip bands that reduce the crack-tip plastic zone, shifting fracture from ductile microvoid coalescence toward quasi-cleavage and lowering plane-strain fracture toughness.
generation.material_initial_state: Single-phase, equiatomic or near-equiatomic FCC HEA (e.g., Co–Cr–Fe–Mn–Ni family), solutionized and water-quenched to minimize SRO; recrystallized, grain size 10–50 µm; clean boundaries without detectable second phases.
generation.intervention: Induce intragranular SRO without forming second phases or grain-boundary precipitates via isothermal aging at an intermediate temperature that promotes SRO (e.g., 350–550 °C depending on alloy) for controlled times; maintain grain size by prior stabilization and short aging; prepare a matched control that is solutionized and quenched to suppress SRO.
generation.conditions: Mechanical testing under inert atmosphere at room temperature and cryogenic temperature (77 K), quasi-static loading (K-rate ~0.1–1 MPa√m/s) in plane strain (ASTM E1820 geometry). Characterize SRO and microstructure at room temperature; verify absence of GB precipitation/segregation before testing.
generation.structural_mediator: Magnitude and correlation length of chemical SRO (Warren–Cowley parameters α_ij and their correlation length), and the associated spatial distribution (width) of local SFE; these mediate slip planarity and crack-tip strain-hardening capacity.
generation.mechanism: SRO preferentially arranges unlike pairs and clusters that lower SFE locally and raise the athermal friction stress inhomogeneously. This suppresses cross-slip and promotes planar, long mean-free-path dislocation glide, producing channelized deformation. At a crack tip, channelization reduces geometrically necessary dislocation storage and crack-tip work hardening, shrinking the plastic zone and facilitating quasi-cleavage along intersecting slip planes. The net effect is a decrease in toughness even without grain-boundary precipitation or coarsening.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the solutionized, low-SRO baseline: (i) yield strength increases modestly; (ii) strain-hardening rate and uniform elongation decrease; (iii) plane-strain fracture toughness KJIc decreases measurably (order 20–40% reduction) at room temperature and more at 77 K; (iv) fracture surfaces show increased quasi-cleavage/river patterns and fewer deep dimples; (v) slip becomes more planar with longer, persistent bands; (vi) diffuse scattering intensity and 3D-ΔPDF/APT pair-correlation signatures of SRO increase; (vii) no grain-boundary precipitates or thick complexion films are detected. Upon heating above the SRO dissolution regime, toughness and ductility recover toward baseline.
generation.baseline: Same alloy in a solutionized-and-quenched state with minimal SRO, matched grain size and boundary chemistry, showing high toughness with dimpled ductile fracture and non-planar (more wavy/cross-slipping) dislocation activity.
generation.boundary: Most pronounced for FCC HEAs with moderate-to-low average SFE and strong negative pair interactions that favor SRO; grain sizes where slip bands can traverse (≥ a few micrometers). Embrittlement intensifies at low temperature and high strain rate (reduced cross-slip and limited dynamic recovery). Diminishes at temperatures where SRO weakens/dissolves or when grains are ultrafine (slip-band truncation). Hydrogen- or impurity-charged conditions can superimpose grain-boundary effects and confound attribution.
generation.uncertainty: Exact SRO thermal window and kinetics are alloy-specific; the magnitude of toughness reduction depends on SRO strength and correlation length. Twinning interactions with SRO may offset or amplify planarity depending on SFE. Weak, undetected boundary complexions could contribute in some chemistries.

falsification_experiment.design: From a single FCC HEA heat, prepare two microstructurally matched batches: (A) solutionize at high temperature and water-quench to minimize SRO; (B) age at an intermediate temperature to create SRO without precipitates. Verify: identical grain size; absence of GB precipitation/films by STEM-EDS/EELS and correlative atom probe tomography (APT) across boundaries; quantify SRO by synchrotron diffuse scattering (3D-ΔPDF) and intragranular APT pair correlations. Test both states for KJIc at RT and 77 K (ASTM E1820), tensile stress–strain, and perform fractography and slip character analysis (EBSD slip-trace statistics, TEM dislocation structures).
measurements: Synchrotron X-ray/neutron diffuse scattering to quantify SRO intensity and correlation length
APT pair correlation functions for key element pairs; boundary vs interior composition profiles
STEM-EDS/EELS of grain boundaries to exclude precipitates/complexions
KJIc (and J–R curves) at RT and 77 K under plane strain
Tensile curves (yield strength, n-value, uniform elongation)
Fractography (fraction of quasi-cleavage vs dimples) and crack-tip plastic zone size via DIC or HR-EBSD
Slip planarity metrics (slip-trace density/length; dislocation character in TEM)
Grain size distribution before and after aging
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If batch B (SRO-present, no GB phases) does not show a statistically significant decrease in KJIc and shift toward planar slip/quasi-cleavage relative to batch A, despite verified higher SRO, the hypothesis is falsified. Alternatively, if a decrease in toughness in batch B only occurs when GB precipitation/segregation is detected, the mechanism is falsified in favor of conventional GB-controlled embrittlement.
